title: Water Turtle Diet Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate exact weekly food portions for aquatic turtles by weight & age. Vet-aligned feeding schedule, gram amounts, and diet breakdown.
intro:
Feeding a pet water turtle sounds simple until you realize that the difference between a thriving 20-year-old red-eared slider and one that dies at 6 from fatty liver disease often comes down to grams and frequency. Most turtle owners rely on vague advice like "feed what the turtle eats in 15 minutes" — a method that works only if you already know your turtle's appetite isn't distorted by boredom, temperature fluctuations, or competition in a multi-turtle tank. This calculator replaces guesswork with a weight-based, age-adjusted feeding prescription used as the standard baseline by reptile veterinarians and herpetological societies worldwide.

The core principle is deceptively straightforward: aquatic turtles should consume roughly **1–3% of their body weight per feeding session**, with the exact percentage and session frequency shifting substantially as the animal matures. A 50-gram hatchling needs daily feeding at the high end of that range to fuel explosive skeletal and shell growth. A 900-gram adult painted turtle eating daily at the same rate will accumulate fat deposits around its organs within months — even if it looks energetic and eager at feeding time. Turtles have no satiety signal that humans can easily read, and their begging behavior is completely decoupled from nutritional need.

What makes this calculator different from generic "feed as much as fits in the turtle's head" advice is the translation of that rule into **actual gram quantities** tied to a verified body weight. It also accounts for the three distinct life stages — hatchling (under 1 year), juvenile (1–4 years), and adult (5+ years) — each with its own sessions-per-week schedule and protein-to-vegetation ratio recommendation. Knowing that your specific 340-gram, 2-year-old slider needs approximately 6–7 grams per session, three to four times per week, lets you pre-portion food, brief a house-sitter accurately, compare the cost-efficiency of pellet brands, and catch overfeeding early by noticing when your turtle's weight gain outpaces the expected growth curve.

Chronic overfeeding is the single most documented cause of premature death in captive aquatic turtles, with pyramiding shell deformity, metabolic bone disease, and hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver) as the three most common consequences. Underfeeding — typically caused by excessive restraint in adult turtles that owners have already over-fattened — causes immune suppression and increased susceptibility to respiratory infections and shell rot. The narrow optimal band between those two failure modes is exactly what this tool is designed to help you find and maintain consistently, regardless of whether your turtle is a newly acquired hatchling or a decade-old breeding adult.
keyTakeaway: **Weekly food (grams) = Body Weight (g) × feeding-rate% × sessions/week**, e.g., a 400 g juvenile at 2% per session × 4 sessions = ~32 g/week total.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

The calculator uses a **two-factor feeding formula** based on body weight percentage, modulated by an age-dependent feeding rate and session frequency:

```
Daily_Portion_g  = Body_Weight_g × Feeding_Rate
Weekly_Portion_g = Daily_Portion_g × Sessions_Per_Week

Where:
  Feeding_Rate     = 0.030 (hatchling, 0–1 yr)
                   = 0.020 (juvenile,  1–4 yrs)
                   = 0.015 (sub-adult, 4–7 yrs)
                   = 0.010 (adult,     7+ yrs)

  Sessions_Per_Week = 7  (hatchling)
                    = 4  (juvenile)
                    = 3  (sub-adult / adult)
```

**Example A – 50 g hatchling (0.5 yrs):**
`50 × 0.030 × 7 = 10.5 g/week`

**Example B – 400 g juvenile (2 yrs):**
`400 × 0.020 × 4 = 32 g/week`

**Example C – 800 g adult (8 yrs):**
`800 × 0.010 × 3 = 24 g/week`

---

## Reference Table

| Age Stage | Age Range | Body Weight (typical) | Feeding Rate (% BW/session) | Sessions/Week | Example Weekly Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hatchling | 0 – 1 yr | 10 – 80 g | 3.0 % | 7 | ~10–17 g |
| Juvenile | 1 – 4 yrs | 80 – 500 g | 2.0 % | 4 | ~6–40 g |
| Sub-adult | 4 – 7 yrs | 500 – 900 g | 1.5 % | 3 | ~23–41 g |
| Adult | 7+ yrs | 900 – 2,000+ g | 1.0 % | 3 | ~27–60 g |

*Typical weights for red-eared sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans), the most commonly kept US water turtle species.*

---

## Diet Composition (What to Feed)

Proper nutrition isn't just about quantity — the diet split matters enormously:

| Life Stage | Commercial Pellets | Leafy Greens | Live/Frozen Protein |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hatchling | 50 % | 10 % | 40 % (feeder fish, bloodworms) |
| Juvenile | 50 % | 25 % | 25 % |
| Sub-adult | 40 % | 40 % | 20 % |
| Adult | 30 % | 50 % | 20 % |

As turtles age, they naturally shift toward a more herbivorous diet. Adults that receive too much protein develop kidney stress.

---

## Typical Cases

**Case 1 – Newly acquired red-eared slider, 35 g, ~4 months old:**
Hatchling rate applies: `35 × 0.03 × 7 = 7.35 g/week`. Split into 7 small daily feedings of ~1 g each. Offer 40% protein (bloodworms or small feeder shrimp) + 50% high-quality pellets (e.g., ReptoMin).

**Case 2 – Painted turtle, 320 g, 3 years old:**
Juvenile rate: `320 × 0.02 × 4 = 25.6 g/week`. Feed every other day (~6.4 g per session). Diet: 50% pellets, 25% romaine/dandelion greens, 25% cooked chicken or freeze-dried shrimp.

**Case 3 – Large female red-eared slider, 1,200 g, 10 years old:**
Adult rate: `1200 × 0.01 × 3 = 36 g/week`. Feed 3×/week (~12 g per session). Shift diet to 50% greens (collard, mustard, waterweed), 30% pellets, 20% protein.

---

## Common Errors

1. **Feeding by eye, not by weight** — "a pinch" is meaningless and leads to systematic overfeeding by 50–200%. Always tare a kitchen scale.
2. **Using adult frequency for hatchlings** — Feeding a 3-month-old only 3×/week causes stunted growth and metabolic bone disease due to calcium deficiency during critical shell formation.
3. **Ignoring the herbivory shift** — Keeping an adult turtle on a 40% protein diet strains kidneys. Protein-induced gout is a documented condition in adult captive sliders.
4. **Counting water lettuce as "food"** — Aquatic plants like duckweed and water lettuce are enrichment/grazing, not part of the calculated portion. Don't subtract them from the daily gram target.
5. **Feeding in the living enclosure without a divider tank** — Uneaten food in the main tank spikes ammonia within hours. Always feed in a separate container or remove uneaten food within 15–20 minutes.
6. **Not adjusting after weight gain** — Recalculate every 3 months for growing turtles. A juvenile that grew from 150 g to 300 g in 6 months needs a completely new portion calculation.

faq.q: How much should I feed a red-eared slider by weight, exactly?
faq.a: The standard veterinary guideline is 1–3% of the turtle's body weight per feeding session, with the specific percentage depending on life stage. Hatchlings (under 1 year) eat at the 2.5–3% end of that range daily, because their shell and skeletal development requires sustained high caloric input. Juveniles (1–4 years) drop to 2–2.5% per session but eat 4 sessions per week rather than 7. Adults (5+ years) fall to 1–1.5% per session at 3 sessions per week. Concretely: a 200-gram juvenile slider gets approximately 4–5 grams per session, four times per week, totaling 16–20 grams weekly. Always weigh food on a 0.1-gram digital kitchen scale for accuracy — visual estimation of pellets can be off by 40–60% depending on pellet size and brand, which accumulates into meaningful overfeeding over weeks.

faq.q: What is the 'head-sized portion' rule, and how accurate is it really?
faq.a: The head-sized portion rule states you should offer the turtle an amount of food roughly equal to the volume of its head (without the neck). It's a practical field heuristic developed for situations where you don't have a scale — it does correlate loosely with body-weight-based portions because head volume scales with body mass. However, it has meaningful limitations: it doesn't account for food density differences between bloodworms (very light) and pellets (dense), it's subjective and prone to owner generosity, and it provides no guidance on session frequency. For casual turtle keepers without access to a scale, it's a useful ceiling — "no more than this" — but it should not replace gram-based portioning when precision matters, especially for turtles already showing weight-related health issues. This calculator converts that concept into verifiable gram quantities.

faq.q: Can you overfeed a water turtle, and what does it look like?
faq.a: Yes, and overfeeding is the most frequently documented cause of premature death in captive aquatic turtles. The visible signs include: (1) pyramiding — scutes developing raised, pyramid-like bumps rather than a smooth, uniform shell surface, caused by excessively rapid growth from excess protein; (2) skin rolls or "fat pockets" visible around the front leg openings when the turtle retracts into its shell or when held upright; (3) a shell that appears disproportionately large relative to the turtle's ability to fully retract. Internally, overfed turtles develop hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver disease), which progresses silently and is often only diagnosed at necropsy. Reptile veterinarians note that captive turtles fed ad libitum or on enriched hatchling-stage diets past juvenility can have their lifespans cut from 30–40 years to under 10. If you notice any of the visual signs above, reduce weekly gram total by 20–25% and recheck weight in 8 weeks.

faq.q: How should the protein-to-vegetable ratio change as my turtle ages?
faq.a: The shift is dramatic and one of the most commonly mismanaged aspects of turtle husbandry. Hatchlings (0–12 months) require approximately 50–60% animal protein — bloodworms, brine shrimp, small feeder insects, and high-protein micro-pellets — because rapid bone and shell mineralization demands dense amino acid availability alongside calcium. Juveniles (1–4 years) drop to 25–35% protein as growth rate slows. Adults (5+ years) should ideally receive 40–50% leafy dark greens (romaine, dandelion greens, red-leaf lettuce, collard greens), 25–35% quality commercial pellets, and only 15–20% animal protein. Continuing a hatchling's protein-heavy diet into adulthood is a primary driver of kidney disease in red-eared sliders, which is the species most commonly presented to exotic vets with renal failure. The transition isn't abrupt — gradually shift ratios over 2–3 months at each life-stage boundary.

faq.q: Do water turtles need UVB light, and how does it affect their dietary calcium needs?
faq.a: UVB light is not optional — it is a non-negotiable dietary requirement in the sense that without it, no amount of calcium-rich food will be properly metabolized. UVB radiation (specifically UVB-B at 290–315 nm wavelength) triggers vitamin D3 synthesis in the turtle's skin, and D3 is the essential co-factor that allows calcium absorption from the gut. Without sufficient UVB, a turtle eating a calcium-adequate diet will still develop metabolic bone disease (MBD) because the calcium passes through unabsorbed. Use a fluorescent or mercury vapor UVB bulb rated for reptiles (Zoo Med Reptisun 5.0 or 10.0 for semi-aquatic species), position it so the basking spot receives full-spectrum exposure within the bulb's effective range (typically 12–18 inches), and replace bulbs every 6–12 months even if they still emit visible light — UVB output degrades well before the visible light does. If UVB access is inadequate, calcium supplementation must include vitamin D3 in the powder; if UVB is reliable and strong, use calcium powder without D3 to avoid hypervitaminosis D.

faq.q: How does water temperature affect how much and how often I should feed my turtle?
faq.a: Water turtles are ectotherms, meaning their metabolic rate — including digestion — is entirely temperature-dependent. At optimal tank temperatures (75–80°F / 24–27°C for red-eared sliders and most North American aquatic species), use the full feeding schedule the calculator provides. As water temperature drops below 70°F (21°C), digestive enzyme activity slows, and you should reduce session frequency by one per week. Below 60°F (15°C), cease feeding entirely — food will sit undigested in the gut, rot, and cause fatal septicemia or cloacal impaction. Conversely, a turtle maintained above optimal temperature (common in summer or with malfunctioning heaters) will have elevated metabolism and may appear hungrier than normal; resist overfeeding in response, as increased appetite from heat does not require proportionally increased rations. Always verify your basking spot reaches 88–92°F (31–33°C) so the turtle can thermoregulate after feeding and fully activate digestive processes.

faq.q: What commercial pellet brands do reptile vets actually recommend?
faq.a: The two most consistently recommended options by reptile veterinarians and accredited zoological institutions are Mazuri Freshwater Turtle Diet and Zoo Med ReptoMin. Both formulations are nutritionally profiled for semi-aquatic species, with Mazuri typically running approximately 32% crude protein and 5% crude fat, suitable for growth stages. ReptoMin's floating sticks are often preferred for juvenile turtles because the sticks reduce the turtle's need to dive for food, making portion observation easier. Neither product should constitute more than 40–50% of total diet — they are designed as a base, not a sole food source. Avoid generic aquarium pellets, goldfish pellets, and koi sticks, which typically lack adequate vitamin D3, calcium, and have protein profiles calibrated for fish metabolism, not chelonians. If cost is a factor, Fluker's Buffet Blend and Tetra ReptoMin offer acceptable but somewhat less optimal nutritional profiles at lower price points.

faq.q: How do I know if my turtle is at a healthy weight without a vet visit?
faq.a: The most reliable home assessment is the retraction test: hold the turtle vertically with the head pointing downward. A healthy-weight turtle should be able to retract all four limbs and head into the shell without obvious folds of skin or fatty tissue bulging from the leg openings. Visible skin rolls — particularly around the front limbs — indicate excess fat deposits. Conversely, if the limb skin appears loose, wrinkled like a deflated balloon, or if you can see bony ridges around the neck and shoulders, the turtle is underweight. For weight tracking, weigh monthly on a digital kitchen scale (tared with a small bowl for the turtle to sit in) and plot against published species growth charts: a healthy female red-eared slider at age 3 should weigh approximately 250–450 grams; at age 5, approximately 500–800 grams, depending on diet quality and genetics. Deviations of more than 20% from expected range warrant a veterinary consultation.

faq.q: Can water turtles eat fruits, and are there any foods I should never offer?
faq.a: Fruits should be offered only as very occasional treats (once or twice monthly at most) for adult turtles and avoided entirely for hatchlings and juveniles. Fruits are high in simple sugars and phosphorus relative to calcium — the inverse of what aquatic turtles need — and frequent fruit feeding disrupts the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio in the diet, contributing to MBD over time. Citrus specifically should be avoided entirely, as the acidity irritates the gastrointestinal tract. Foods to never feed include: any dairy product (turtles cannot digest lactose), raw meat from mammals (high in saturated fat and often carries Salmonella in conditions lethal to turtles), iceberg lettuce (nutritionally empty and causes diarrhea), spinach and beet greens (oxalate content binds calcium and prevents absorption), fireflies and other luminescent insects (toxic to all reptiles, causing rapid death), and avocado (persin content is toxic to many reptile species). Safe protein sources include earthworms, mealworms in moderation, aquatic snails, small feeder fish (not goldfish — their thiaminase content depletes vitamin B1 over time), freeze-dried or live brine shrimp, and repashy aquatic gel diets.

faq.q: Do water turtles hibernate, and should I stop feeding before brumation?
faq.a: Wild aquatic turtles in temperate climates undergo brumation — a cold-induced metabolic slowdown distinct from true mammalian hibernation — during winter months, typically October through March in North America. Captive turtles maintained at stable warm temperatures year-round technically do not need to brumate, and most reptile veterinarians recommend against forcing brumation in pet turtles unless breeding is a goal, because the controlled captive environment makes it safer to maintain normal temperature and feeding year-round. If you do allow or facilitate brumation (outdoor pond turtles in seasonal climates), begin reducing feeding frequency 3–4 weeks before expected brumation onset and transition to easily digestible foods. Feed the last meal approximately 2–3 weeks before the turtle's anticipated temperature drop so the gut is fully empty before metabolism slows to the point where digestion halts. Undigested food during brumation causes fatal bacterial proliferation in the gastrointestinal tract. Post-brumation, recalibrate your feeding calculator to the turtle's actual current weight — significant muscle and fat mass can be lost over winter.

faq.q: How should I feed multiple turtles of different sizes and ages in the same tank?
faq.a: Multi-turtle feeding is one of the most common sources of chronic under- and overfeeding in hobbyist setups, because dominant or faster-moving turtles monopolize food regardless of their own dietary needs. The only reliable method is temporary separation feeding: remove each turtle individually to a small separate bin or secondary tank (without filtration — a clean plastic tub works) filled with 2–3 inches of tank water, offer the pre-portioned gram amount calculated for that specific turtle, allow 15–20 minutes of feeding, then return the turtle. This ensures each animal receives its precise allocation and allows you to monitor appetite changes in each individual — which is an early diagnostic indicator for illness, as sick turtles refuse food before showing other symptoms. Never feed turtles in their main display tank if accurate portion control matters, as food particles not consumed will dissolve and spike ammonia levels regardless of filtration capacity. For households where daily separation is impractical, feed the smallest/youngest turtle first in the main tank and monitor closely, removing uneaten food aggressively.

faq.q: Is it normal for a water turtle to refuse food for several days, and when should I be concerned?
faq.a: Short-term food refusal (2–5 days) is normal and common in several situations: immediately after transport or rehoming stress (allow 1–2 weeks for acclimation before adjusting feeding protocols), during temperature fluctuations when the tank drops below 70°F, during shedding cycles when turtles may be uncomfortable, and in females during pre-oviposition periods when gravitational pressure from developing eggs reduces appetite. Seasonal light changes can also trigger appetite reduction in turtles near windows even if tank temperature is stable. Refusal becomes a veterinary concern when it extends beyond 2–3 weeks with no environmental explanation, when it's accompanied by visible lethargy (turtle not basking, staying submerged unusually long), abnormal feces (white/chalky, bloody, or gelatinous), visible shell changes (softening, unusual discoloration, lesions), or wheezing or nasal discharge suggesting respiratory infection. The most common medical causes of appetite loss in water turtles are respiratory infections, intestinal parasites, vitamin A deficiency (hypovitaminosis A), and internal abscess formation. Any sustained refusal combined with even one additional symptom warrants an exotic animal veterinary evaluation within 5–7 days.
